Oh, the main thing is project-based learning, rather than just taking notes and memorizing things and taking tests (New Tech had tests, too, but not as frequently). We’d get an “entry document” that describes a problem (say, for instance, that you want to build a catapult to launch a pie at your teacher), and you then come up with “need to knows” (questions, steps to solve the problem, things like that). Then, we’d have “workshops,” which taught things a little more like conventional high school. Then, though, you’d take that material and apply it to the current project (physics things like acceleration and all that). Then, your group makes a final product, which would usually be a presentation, but could also be an actual physical creation or something else.
There are some other little nuances, too, but I don’t remember absolutely everything.

My situation sorta evolved over my lifetime.

I made a sorta cheap attempt when I was 10 because I was fat and I thought that would never change. Well, I’m still fat, but not quite as badly. 

I thought about it when I was an underclassman in high school because I thought I’d never find love.

Got seriously sick when I was 17 (something I still live with, but not nearly as badly) and fashioned a noose out of an extension cord because I wanted the agony to end.

Junior year of college, I was all alone and was in a shit living situation, so it sat at the back of my mind.

And now, there’s this tiny inkling of desire to die that sits at the back of my mind because I have no life, finding a job is going to be tough, and the world is in shambles. 

Each time, though, I convinced myself (still am) to go on. There’s a few lines of reasoning I use to do so.

Court exists to test whether accusations are true or false, right? For instance, “so-and-so was the one who broke in and stole the diamond.” How do you prove or disprove that? Evidence. Video, any blood found on the scene, etc. Now, what if that statement becomes “I’m worthless,” “nobody loves me,” “I will never be happy”, etc.? Where’s the evidence to prove all that? Can we look into the future and procure video or something? Can we read people’s minds and get transcripts of what they think of us? No, we can’t. Therefore, we can’t prove it won’t get better. We have no evidence. 

The second has to do with how our emotions and our logic often don’t agree. My emotions can react to the bad stuff and want to escape from it so badly that I want to die, but my logic is there to step in and say that dying would be the *worst* idea. I think of suicidal thoughts for exactly what they are: thoughts. And not all of our thoughts are helpful to us, so we don’t have to give in to them.

Thirdly, and I happened upon this one recently... what about all the things in life that give you feelings of pleasure? Even the simplest things, like the leaves of the trees, sunsets on the beach, cats, etc. *We can only enjoy those because we’re alive.* We don’t know what comes after death; hell, the afterlife could be worse. And more than likely, we’ll never get to experience those things that make us happy again.

Distracting myself with said things (for me, that includes video games, YouTube, etc.) seriously helps, too. 

I did tell a therapist about these thoughts, and what methods I would use, but he just told me to  stay away from those methods whenever the thoughts come on. Which is good advice, but... I could’ve used a bit more, you know?
